## Close Reading of Sir Walter Scott's *The Pirate*

---

### 1. What Happens, Scene by Scene

**Paratextual Frame**: The text opens with the title page, illustration list, and two introductions: Andrew Lang's extensive Editor's Introduction (discussing composition, sources, and reception) and Scott's own Author's Introduction describing the 1814 lighthouse-commission voyage. An Advertisement provides the historical account of John Gow the pirate, establishing the fictional frame.

**Chapter I**: Scott establishes Jarlshof, a ruined mansion at Sumburgh-Head, describing its Norwegian origins now buried in sand. Basil Mertoun, a mysterious Englishman, arrives and takes tenancy from Magnus Troil, the Norwegian-descended Udaller (allodial proprietor). Mertoun is taciturn, abstemious, and lives in gloomy seclusion with his son Mordaunt.

**Chapter II**: Mertoun's household management reveals his fierce temper when his housekeeper Swertha overcharges a fisherman; he dismisses her but she returns on Mordaunt's counsel. Mertoun's "dark hour" depressions isolate him for days; Mordaunt learns to absent himself during these fits, spending time among the Zetlanders.

**Chapter III**: Introduction of Magnus Troil's daughters: Minna (dark-haired, grave, imaginative) and Brenda (fair, gay, lively). Mordaunt has grown up with them but shows no exclusive attachment to either. The public expects him to marry one.

**Chapter IV**: Mordaunt departs Burgh-Westra during storm warnings. He seeks shelter at Harfra, home of Triptolemus Yellowley, the new Scottish agricultural factor, whose sister Barbara blocks the door.

**Chapter V**: The Yellowleys keep doors bolted—a Scottish peculiarity that offends Zetland hospitality. Mordaunt forces entry. Triptolemus is learned but impractical; Barbara is penurious. Norna of the Fitful-Head arrives, threatening doom. She chants the Reimkennar, a Runic wind-charm, and the storm abates—leaving the Yellowleys astonished.

**Chapter VI**: Norna departs; Mordaunt leaves after dinner, meeting the pedlar Bryce Snailsfoot. He reaches Jarlshof to find his father recovered from a dark hour.

**Chapter VII**: Mordaunt and his father climb Sumburgh-Head. A wreck drifts past—Mordaunt descends the cliff face and rescues a half-drowned sailor. Bryce Snailsfoot refuses aid, citing the superstition that saving drowning men brings harm. Norna appears and commands him to help. The stranger is taken to the Ranzelman Neil Ronaldson's house.

**Chapter VIII**: Clement Cleveland, captain of the lost vessel *Good Hope* of Bristol, recovers. He is blunt, nautical, and gives Mordaunt a Spanish rifle. He speaks of a consort ship and intends to stay at Burgh-Westra.

**Chapter IX**: Mordaunt broods on his eclipse at Burgh-Westra. He meets Norna at Green Loch, who warns that a serpent has crept into Magnus Troil's household and that Cleveland threatens Minna. She commands him to attend the St. John's Eve festival.

**Chapter X**: Triptolemus Yellowley, with sister Barbara, journeys to Burgh-Westra, discussing improvements with Mordaunt. Triptolemus falls from his pony into a mill-stream, muttering about Lanarkshire cows.

**Chapter XI**: Arrival at Burgh-Westra. Magnus gives Mordaunt a cold welcome. Minna and Brenda receive him with guarded courtesy. Cleveland dominates the household.

**Chapter XII**: The feast assembles. Mordaunt sits between the Groatsettar sisters, observing Minna's exclusive attention to Cleveland and Brenda's restless glances toward him. The sword-dance concludes with Minna as "Queen of Swords."

**Chapter XIII**: Drinking revels. Triptolemus proposes reforms; Magnus mockingly threatens him with sea-water. Halcro tells his story of meeting Dryden. The Udaller silences innovation.

**Chapter XIV**: Halcro recites "The Song of Harold Harfager." Triptolemus quarrels about ploughs and weights. The sword-dance is performed, Minna most distinguished.

**Chapter XV**: Masquers arrive as Tritons and Nereids—actually local guests including Halcro's design. Brenda signals Mordaunt privately.

**Chapter XVI**: Under moonlight, Brenda reveals that Norna sent her. She warns that Cleveland endangers Minna. They acknowledge renewed friendship. Mordaunt realizes his feelings for Brenda.

**Chapter XVII**: A whale strands in the voe. Triptolemus throws his graip injudiciously; the whale escapes. Cleveland swims to save Mordaunt after his boat capsizes, then coldly refuses thanks, suggesting a duel: "sixty yards of the sea-beach, and a brace of rifles."

**Chapter XVIII**: Bryce Snailsfoot arrives with news of an armed vessel at Kirkwall—possibly Cleveland's consort. Magnus proposes a voyage to Kirkwall fair. Cleveland buys presents liberally, including a mantilla for Barbara.

**Chapter XIX**: Norna appears at midnight in the sisters' bedroom, singing Runic verses. She begins a tale of her father Erland, brother to Magnus's grandfather Olave, involving the Dwarfie Stone of Hoy and dealings with supernatural powers. She warns of a demon and the lamp's fading light. The text breaks off mid-sentence.

### 2. Characters: Who Speaks or Acts and What Drives Them

**Basil Mertoun**: Mysterious, withdrawn, subject to periodic depressions ("dark hours"). His aversion to company, women, and alcohol marks him as a man fleeing a guilty past. He tolerates Magnus Troil's patronage but maintains absolute solitude. His sudden interest in which Troil daughter Mordaunt prefers hints at his own romantic history haunting him.

**Mordaunt Mertoun**: Young, athletic, beloved by Zetlanders, raised partly among them after his father's retreats. His competence in dangerous cliff sports and seamanship contrasts with his intellectual education. His heart "hovers" equally between Minna and Brenda until Brenda's midnight confession crystallizes his preference. He is proud, wounded by neglect, and impulsive—one who "could not forbear laughing" at Swertha's bribery and who challenges the pedlar with a beetle.

**Magnus Troil**: The Udaller—proud, hospitable, conservative, descended from Norwegian earls. He rules his household absolutely and brooks no innovation. His coldness toward Mordaunt, whom he once favored, proves external influence (Cleveland's slanders) has worked upon him. His hearty welcome to strangers and fierce protection of local custom embody the ideal Norse chieftain.

**Minna Troil**: Dark-haired, contemplative, imaginative—drawn to Cleveland's tales of distant lands and dangers. Her "high-wrought tone of enthusiasm" makes her believe in Norna without trembling. She leads the sword-dance with martial grace and shows "the deepest contempt" for old Haagen's cowardice under Montrose. Her attention to Cleveland suggests she mistakes boldness for heroism.

**Brenda Troil**: Fair, gay, practical, more knowing of the world (having visited Lerwick when Dutch ships were there). She disbelieves superstition but trembles at it. Her private interview with Mordaunt reveals loyalty to her sister and nascent love for him. Her "anxiety and trouble" when signaling shows her divided between sisterly duty and personal feeling.

**Clement Cleveland**: Nautical, bold, frank in manner, wealthy (his purse of Spanish pistoles). His "open, naval frankness" and "undoubting confidence" captivate Minna. He saves Mordaunt from drowning, then refuses thanks and hints at a duel—"danger has been my consort for life." His insistence on retrieving the golden chain and silver box suggests personal significance beyond their value.

**Norna of the Fitful-Head**: Haughty, commanding, claiming supernatural power over winds. Scott carefully leaves ambiguous whether she is "impostor or enthusiast"—she acts with "undoubting confidence" yet shows "deeply-rooted mental affliction." Her relation to the Troil family (distant, once romantic) explains her investment. Her warning to Mordaunt and midnight visit to the sisters show protective purpose.

**Triptolemus Yellowley**: Scottish factor, "dour" and "intractable" in farming, obsessed with agricultural improvement. His classical education ("_Operam et oleum perdidi_") mixes absurdly with practical ignorance. He falls into the mill-stream, proposes Scots measures, and gets mocked by Magnus. His sister Barbara's penury contrasts with his schemes.

**Claud Halcro**: Aged poet, descendant of Haco Goldemund, friend to all, keeper of Norse songs. His "hobby-horse" is his meeting with Dryden, which he recounts constantly. His verses ("The Song of Harold Harfager") keep Norse tradition alive. He loves "wit and song" and defends the old ways against Triptolemus's innovations.

**Bryce Snailsfoot**: Pedlar, "green-glazen eyes," combines profit-seeking with superstitious caution. He refuses to aid drowning men, overcharges, and sells smuggled goods. Yet he serves as information conduit between islands.

### 3. Four Passages Worth Quoting

**Passage 1** (Opening description, establishing setting):

> "That long, narrow, and irregular island, usually called the mainland of Zetland, because it is by far the largest of that Archipelago, terminates, as is well known to the mariners who navigate the stormy seas which surround the Thule of the ancients, in a cliff of immense height, entitled Sumburgh-Head, which presents its bare scalp and naked sides to the weight of a tremendous surge, forming the extreme point of the isle to the south-east."

This passage establishes Scott's method: precise geographical naming ("Thule of the ancients") merges with empirical description. The personification ("bare scalp and naked sides") gives the landscape personality. The syntax—compound sentences with subordinate clauses—mimics the coast's irregularity. The "tremendous surge" prepares for the maritime action to come and frames Zetland as a place where nature overwhelms human habitation.

**Passage 2** (Norna's wind-charm, supernatural thematization):

> "'Stern eagle of the far north-west, / Thou that bearest in thy grasp the thunderbolt...'"

The Reimkennar invokes natural forces as a personified eagle. The verse structure (four-line stanzas, trochaic rhythm) imitates Old Norse verse. Norna's command ("Hear the voice of the Reim-kennar") positions her as equal to elemental power. The storm's cessation immediately after—whether natural or supernatural—remains ambiguous, embodying Scott's technique of "rational explanation" that carries "probabilit[y] almost equal to an absolute goblin narrative." The charm establishes Norse spiritual heritage as active force.

**Passage 3** (Triptolemus and the whale, comedy and cultural clash):

> "'I tell you, Master Yellowley,' said the Udaller, 'that every man who risks his life to bring that fish ashore, shall have an equal share and partition, according to our ancient and loveable Norse custom and wont; nay, if there is so much as a woman looking on, that will but touch the cable, she will be partner with us; ay, and more than all that, if she will but say there is a reason for it, we will assign a portion to the babe that is unborn.'
